newsitem.title: DUBAI: Politics not economics puts Yemen GCC bid on hold.
newsitem.headline: Politics not economics puts Yemen GCC bid on hold.

text.p: A response expected next week to Yemen's bid to join the elite club of six wealthy Gulf Arab states will not go beyond granting the impoverished country a favourable status, diplomats and analysts said on Monday.
"Denial of full membership will be very diplomatic. The Gulf club is not open for new members," said a Gulf-based analyst.
"The most that Yemen could hope for is an observer position or an arrangement along the lines of a most favoured nation."

The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) formed in 1981 groups all the other countries of the Arabian peninsula between the Gulf and the Red Sea -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Oman.
UAE media said on Monday Qatar's Cabinet Affairs Minister Mohammad bin Khalid al-Thani would visit Sanaa next week to deliver the GCC response to Yemen's application.

Yemen's Minister for Legal and Parliamentary Affairs Abdullah Ahmad Ghanem in December delivered the membership request to the Emir of Qatar Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani whose country hosted the annual GCC summit.
Analysts said it was a tactical move by President Ali Abdullah Saleh to stress Yemen's claims to a legal right to join the Gulf alliance.

Ghanem had said earlier in an interview with Yemeni media that his country qualified for membership on the basis of its geographic location in the Arabian peninsula and its historical ties with GCC states.
Gulf-based diplomats said the UAE, Oman and Qatar favoured Yemen's admission, but stopped short of pushing the issue further as arguments about risks and the council's homogeneous structure surfaced.
"Admitting a revolutionary republic with socialist roots into a capitalist gathering of one kingdom, one sultanate and four emirates could make Gulf leaders uncomfortable," said one analyst.
Yemen is the only country in the Arabian peninsula with political parties, opposition newspapers and active Islamist participation in government.
The Republic of Yemen was formed in May 1990 by the merger of the conservative North Yemen and the Marxist South Yemen following hundreds of years of separation.

Saleh first became North Yemen's president in 1978. Of his four predecessors since North Yemen became a republic in 1962, three were assassinated while in office and the fourth resigned before completing his term.

Yemen has ironed out differences with most Gulf Arab states over its support for Baghdad during Iraq's 1990-91 occupation of Kuwait and made progress in resolving a 60-year border dispute with Saudi Arabia, the council's dominant power.

Analysts said Yemeni leaders believed a firm, stable and unified Yemen after Saleh's success in crushing a 1994 secessionist bid by leaders of the former South Yemen boosted their chances of qualifying for full GCC membership.
They said Yemeni leaders believed that reforms, increased oil production and gas projects would eliminate economic reservations by council members.
"Yemen is coming out of the economic bottle-neck. In a few years it will not be a burden to the deficit-ridden member states," a Gulf columnist said.

Yemen, a small independent oil producer, also hopes to qualify for membership of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries before the turn of the century, and is aggressively developing a number of liquefied natural gas projects.
"Yemen's membership in the GCC is strategically feasible. This has been on the mind of American planners for a long time," an Arab affairs journalist wrote in the London-based daily Asharq al-Awsat.

He said the United States believes Yemen to be the southwestern gate to the Gulf and could make possible the deployment of GCC or allied troops at strategic points from the Gulf to Bab al-Mandab at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Diplomats said Sanaa's application was discussed at length at the December summit's closed sessions, but no mention of it was made in the final statement.

The only mention of the Yemeni request was at a news conference by Qatar's Foreign Minister Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jabr al-Thani who ruled out full membership but said a Qatari envoy would deliver a "good" response to Sanaa.
